plain_english: Now let's talk about money and possessions — the biggest source of human misery. If you compare all our other troubles — death, illness, fear, regret, pain, hard work — with the problems that money causes us, money wins by a landslide. Think about this: it hurts much less to never have money than to lose money you once had. This shows us that the less poor people have to lose, the less they can be tortured by loss. You're wrong if you think rich people handle financial losses better than poor people do. A wound hurts the same whether you're big or small. Bion had a clever way of putting it: "Pulling out hair hurts just as much whether you're bald or have a full head of hair." The same is true for rich and poor people — they suffer equally when they lose money. Money sticks to both types of people, and you can't rip it away without them feeling it. But as I said, it's easier to bear never getting something than losing something you had. That's why you'll notice that people who were never lucky are often happier than people who used to be lucky but aren't anymore.
original_excerpt: Let us now pass on to the consideration of property, that most fertile source of human sorrows: for if you compare all the other ills from which we suffer—deaths, sicknesses, fears, regrets, endurance of pains and labours— with those miseries which our money inflicts upon us, the latter will far outweigh all the others. Reflect, then, how much less a grief it is never to have had any money than to have lost it: we shall thus understand that the less poverty has to lose, the less torment it has with which to afflict us: for you are mistaken if you suppose that the rich bear their losses with greater spirit than the poor: a wound causes the same amount of pain to the greatest and the smallest body.

plain_english: Diogenes was a man of great spirit who figured this out. He made it impossible for anyone to take anything from him. Call this freedom from loss whatever you want — poverty, want, necessity, or any insulting name you can think of. I still say this man was happy, unless you can show me another person who has nothing to lose. If I'm right, then among all the greedy people, cheaters, and thieves in the world, being the one person who can't be harmed is almost godlike. Anyone who doubts Diogenes was happy might as well doubt whether the gods themselves are happy enough — after all, they don't own farms or gardens, they don't have valuable estates rented out to tenants, and they don't have big investments in the money market. Aren't you ashamed of yourself for staring at wealth with such amazement? Look at the universe: you'll see the gods own absolutely nothing, yet they give us everything. Do you really think this man who stripped away all the random things fortune gives us is poor? Or is he more like the immortal gods?
original_excerpt: It was a neat saying of Bion’s, “that it hurts bald men as much as hairy men to have their hairs pulled out”: you may be assured that the same thing is true of rich and poor people, that their suffering is equal: for their money clings to both classes, and cannot be torn away without their feeling it: yet it is more endurable, as I have said, and easier not to gain property than to lose it, and therefore you will find that those upon whom Fortune has never smiled are more cheerful than those whom she has deserted. Diogenes, a man of infinite spirit, perceived this, and made it impossible that anything should be taken from him. Call this security from loss poverty, want, necessity, or any contemptuous name you please: I shall consider such a man to be happy, unless you find me another who can lose nothing. If I am not mistaken, it is a royal attribute among so many misers, sharpers, and robbers, to be the one man who cannot be injured. If any one doubts the happiness of Diogenes, he would doubt whether the position of the immortal gods was one of sufficient happiness. because they have no farms or gardens, no valuable estates let to strange tenants, and no large loans in the money market.

plain_english:
Do you think Demetrius was happier? He was Pompey's former slave who became incredibly wealthy. He wasn't even embarrassed that he had more money than Pompey himself. Every day someone brought him a count of how many slaves he owned, like a general getting a report on his army. But really, he deserved nothing more than two assistants and a slightly bigger prison cell than the other slaves.

Compare that to Diogenes. His one slave ran away. When someone pointed the runaway out to him, Diogenes didn't think the man was worth chasing down. "It would be shameful," he said, "if Manes can live without Diogenes, but Diogenes can't live without Manes." It's like he was telling Fortune: "Mind your own business! You have no power over Diogenes anymore. Did my slave run away? No — he left me as a free man."
original_excerpt: Are you not ashamed of yourself, you who gaze upon riches with astonished admiration? Look upon the universe: you will see the gods quite bare of property, and possessing nothing though they give everything. Do you think that this man who has stripped himself of all fortuitous accessories is a pauper, or one like to the immortal gods? Do you call Demetrius, Pompeius’s freedman, a happier man, he who was not ashamed to be richer than Pompeius, who was daily furnished with a list of the number of his slaves, as a general is with that of his army, though he had long deserved that all his riches should consist of a pair of underlings, and a roomier cell than the other slaves? But Diogenes’s only slave ran away from him, and when he was pointed out to Diogenes, he did not think him worth fetching back. “It is a shame,” he said, “that Manes should be able to live without Diogenes, and that Diogenes should not be able to live without Manes.” He seems to me to have said, “Fortune, mind your own business: Diogenes has nothing left that belongs to you.

plain_english: A household full of slaves needs food and clothes. You have to feed all those hungry mouths. You have to buy them clothing and watch their thieving hands. And you have to rely on people who hate you and curse your name. How much happier is the person who owes nothing to anyone — except for things he could easily give up! Since most of us don't have that kind of mental strength, we should at least cut down on our possessions. This way we're less exposed to fortune's attacks. Soldiers who can fit inside their armor are better prepared for war than those whose huge bodies stick out everywhere, making them easy targets. The best amount of wealth is just enough to keep you out of poverty — but not much more than that.
original_excerpt: Did my slave run away? nay, he went away from me as a free man.” A household of slaves requires food and clothing: the bellies of so many hungry creatures have to be filled: we must buy raiment for them, we must watch their most thievish hands, and we must make use of the services of people who weep and execrate us. How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease! Since we, however, have not such strength of mind as this, we ought at any rate to diminish the extent of our property, in order to be less exposed to the assaults of fortune: those men whose bodies can be within the shelter of their armour, are more fitted for war than those whose huge size everywhere extends beyond it, and exposes them to wounds: the best amount of property to have is that which is enough to keep us from poverty, and which yet is not far removed from it.
